use_case.name: Answer order and stock questions
use_case.summary: A generative AI chatbot on the website and phone line to answer customer service contacts. Gated here: the 83% of calls that are "where is my order" (71%) and "is part X in stock at branch Y" (12%). Returns, pricing disputes and technical questions are a separate use case.

intake.problem: Customer service is swamped; hold times average 7 minutes and customers complain.
intake.who: 22 customer service agents; about 9,000 business customers.
intake.today: Agents look up order status in the ERP and tracking on the carrier site. Shipment notification emails were turned off years ago after a bad template went out.
intake.volume: About 600 calls and 250 emails a day. A 500-call sample: 71% order status, 12% stock checks.
intake.cost: 7-minute average hold time. No cost per contact worked out.
intake.wrong_answer: A wrong ship date idles the customer's maintenance crew and can cost the account.
intake.data: ERP (orders, inventory, customers) with a readable reporting database; carrier tracking via the shipping system. Buyer names, phones and emails.
intake.value: CEO goal: save 30% of agent time. No value put on the saved time; no layoffs planned.
intake.sign_off: Ana Ruiz (VP Customer Service, owner), the CEO, IT security, general counsel.

input.evidence: The customer gives a PO or order number, or a part number and a branch.

rules.evidence: Agents follow one rule: look the number up in the ERP and the carrier site.

output.evidence: A lookup: order status, ship date, tracking link, stock on hand.

alternative.evidence: Shipment emails, an order-status page and an IVR lookup by order number would answer most of the 83%, from the same ERP data, with exact answers.

alternative.description: Turn shipment emails back on (order confirmed, shipped with tracking link, delayed with new date) from a reviewed template. Add order lookup by PO or order number to the customer portal and the phone menu. Then a branch stock lookup for signed-in customers, the same way. All of it reads the ERP and carrier data agents already use.

value.evidence: The stated goal is agent hours, which scores 0 alone. But average hold time, 7 minutes today, is a wait customers feel and complain about.

volume.evidence: About 600 calls and 250 emails a day; categories from a counted 500-call sample; no cost per contact.

owner.evidence: Ana Ruiz would own it; the CEO asked for it.

wrong_answer.evidence: Cost is clear (idle crews, lost accounts), but no review step or fallback is defined for a chatbot answer.

availability.evidence: Order status, ship dates, tracking and stock are all in the ERP, the source of truth.

quality.evidence: Not known. Nobody has checked how often ERP promise dates match actual delivery.

access.evidence: ERP team owns it; a reporting database is already readable.

sensitivity.evidence: Buyer names, phones and emails are listed as the personal data involved; no masking or access plan described.

regulations: State consumer privacy laws for buyer contact data

sign_off.needs: Which ERP fields the portal, phone menu and emails expose, how customers are authenticated before seeing an order, and logging.
The shipment email templates and the wording of delay notices.
The call categories that move to self-service and how agents point callers to it.
Read access for the portal and phone menu, and the refresh timing of ship dates.

reasons: 83% of contacts ask for a fact that already sits in the ERP, keyed by an order or part number. That is a lookup, not a judgment, and it scores 0 of 8 on the Simplicity Test.
A chatbot would add model cost and the risk of a confidently wrong ship date to a question that has one exact answer.
Proactive shipment emails stop many of these calls before they happen, which no chatbot can do.
"Save 30% of agent time" is not yet a value. Hold time, 7 minutes today, and the accounts at risk from late or wrong answers are the numbers to track.
Returns, pricing disputes and technical questions (17% of calls) may need judgment. Gate them separately once these calls are gone.

top_risks.risk: ERP promise dates are wrong often enough that proactive emails spread bad dates faster.
top_risks.mitigation: Compare promise dates with carrier delivery for one month before turning on delay emails.

top_risks.risk: A template mistake repeats what got emails turned off years ago.
top_risks.mitigation: Review templates with customer service and counsel, send to 5% of customers first, and watch replies and unsubscribes.

top_risks.risk: Customers keep calling out of habit, so call volume barely moves.
top_risks.mitigation: Put the order link in every confirmation, offer the lookup first in the phone menu, and have agents send the link on each call.

first_build.scope: Shipment emails (confirmed, shipped with tracking, delayed) from a reviewed template, plus order lookup by PO or order number in the customer portal and the phone menu. About six weeks with the ERP team.
first_build.left_out: Any chatbot; the branch stock lookup (next, same pattern); returns, pricing disputes and technical questions, which get their own gate.

measure.metric: "Where is my order" calls per day
measure.target: under 200, with average hold time under 3 minutes

result.human_review: A person reviews every output in the first build.
